resources.title: What a young plant needs — Kindergarten
resources.question: What can evidence tell us about a young plant and light?
resources.summary: Plants have observable structures, while explanations of their needs come from scientific teaching and investigation. Light supplies energy used in making food; soil is not a ready-made meal poured into a plant. Compare the strength of a dated record, a photograph and a planned investigation. Any example data in the lessons are invented for learning and do not describe Glenolia growth or health. This Kindergarten pack develops plant structures, light energy and careful comparison through four connected lessons. All materials can be printed; no learner account, family purchase or field trip is necessary. Teachers choose timing, adjust support and assess the evidence themselves. The lessons contribute to selected content only and do not claim NESA endorsement or complete outcome coverage.

resources.title: Soil under our feet — Kindergarten
resources.question: What do safe material observations tell us, and what is missing?

A reading without a unit, scale or method is incomplete, even when its number looks precise. Observation does not diagnose fertility, contamination, organisms or plant health. This Kindergarten pack develops material properties, models and measurement labels through four connected lessons. resources.title: From material to community: explaining paper’s journey — Years 5–6
resources.question: How can we explain a material process and its limits to our community?
resources.summary: Write a scientific and technological explanation of a generic paper-reprocessing journey. Learners connect sorting, pulping, sheet formation and drying to changes in material, then edit misleading claims about origin or impact. This is a source-labelled industrial model, not a classroom recipe, Glenolia manufacturing record or NSW collection instruction. Four lessons build a diagram, a process explanation, a critical revision and a final text for a younger audience. The pack is print-first, uses no hot water or machinery and contributes selected content only; teachers assess the actual explanation and adapt it to their class.

resources.title: Meet a growing place: maps, sources and questions
resources.question: How can a map help us ask a question that the evidence can answer?
resources.summary: Students build a bounded picture of a developing growing place rather than assuming that a farm photograph explains everything. They locate features, distinguish a report from a direct observation, practise an honest map key and design an answerable place-based question. The classroom route uses a deliberately hypothetical school plot; a permitted school-ground or future farm route adds genuine field observations without pretending that missing information has been measured.

resources.title: What a young plant needs: structure, light and a fair plan
resources.question: How could we investigate a young plant’s needs without confusing a plan with a result?
resources.summary: Students connect visible plant structures with functions, distinguish an observed feature from an explanation and plan a safe light comparison. The Glenolia baseline supplies a real question about careful evidence, not a replicated experiment. A clearly labelled simulated dataset allows analysis when no classroom plant trial is appropriate. Pupils explain why a mean, a photograph and one undated claim cannot stand in for repeated comparable measurements.

resources.title: Soil as a system: separate, compare and question
resources.question: What can separating a model mixture tell us, and what does it leave out?
resources.summary: A safe model mixture helps students explain a separation method using particle properties, then recognise why a real soil is more than a jar of particles. Students calculate recovery and proportions from a labelled simulated dataset, identify missing mass and resist turning one property into a verdict on crop suitability. The emphasis is a reasoned method, transparent source labels and a practical next question, not a soil-treatment recommendation.

resources.title: Water, weather and a young plantation
resources.question: What further evidence would turn a dated reading into a useful investigation?
resources.summary: Students audit the real planting record, plan repeatable environmental observations, represent a clearly labelled simulated dataset and communicate a cautious conclusion. They keep nearby modelled weather, forecasts, an owner report and their own observations distinct. The unit develops sampling and scientific communication without pretending that one baseline establishes growth, irrigation need or a complete school depth study.

resources.title: Living relationships: a model that shows its evidence
resources.question: How can we explain relationships without claiming more than we observed?
resources.summary: Students observe permitted living/non-living features, connect plant structures to resource needs, build a sourced relationship model and examine how a proposed human action might affect it. The unit deliberately separates a directly observed organism, a source-based general explanation and an untested local relationship. Cute garden guides prompt questions but are never used as evidence that particular wildlife or pollination has been recorded at Glenolia.

resources.title: From grower to community: follow the evidence
resources.question: How can we tell a product’s story without confusing branding with origin?
resources.summary: Students follow a hypothetical plant-product chain, distinguish growing, processing, transport and retail roles, compare stakeholder perspectives and produce a traceability card that separates verified information from missing detail. The learning connects farming with community and technology while keeping Glenolia’s developing crop and proposed café separate from operating supply chains. No product tasting, shopping, fragrance demonstration or supplier partnership is assumed.

resources.title: Thoughtful design: make an evidence sign
resources.question: How can a small design help visitors understand what is known and what is still growing?
resources.summary: Students design and test a paper visitor-information sign for a hypothetical growing place. They define users and a communication need, set measurable criteria, compare options and revise a prototype using feedback. Accuracy, readability, access, material use and maintenance are considered together. The product remains a learning prototype, not an actual construction, access-compliance, emergency or commercial signage specification.

resources.title: Our year of evidence: explain what changed
resources.question: How can a portfolio show learning rather than simply collect finished pages?
resources.summary: Students revisit a question from the year, select evidence with known provenance, distinguish the work’s quality from its appearance and explain a meaningful revision. They use a group discussion to moderate source and reasoning checks while producing an individual account of what was learned and what remains unresolved. Reports remain teacher-reviewed programme evidence, not a NESA grade conversion, attendance award or automated judgement.

resources.title: Sampling a place: representativeness and bias
resources.question: When does a small sample give a misleading picture of a place?
resources.summary: Students compare sampling frames and strategies using a complete hypothetical population, then design a bounded school-ground or future permitted field inquiry. They quantify how convenient selections can differ from a known model population and explain why a sample is not automatically representative because it is easy, large or called random. The real planting report provides a source-quality case; its 27 plants are not recast as a random trial.

resources.title: Design a plant investigation: causal claims and confounding
resources.question: What would make a light investigation capable of supporting a fair explanation?
resources.summary: Students develop an investigable hypothesis, distinguish biological replication from repeated readings and examine change scores in a small simulated plant experiment. They plan suitable care, random allocation and comparable methods, while recognising that a plan or supplied dataset does not demonstrate conducting a practical investigation. The real Paraíso baseline remains a separate owner report, not an experimental control or treatment group.

resources.title: Soil evidence: method, recovery and uncertainty
resources.question: How do method choices shape the soil story a dataset appears to tell?
resources.summary: Students evaluate simplified material tests, process recovery and flow data and distinguish measurement resolution from accuracy. They identify what a method actually measures before interpreting a result. Simulated separation and water-throughput examples teach comparison without claiming to establish real soil health, plant-available water or a prescription for the Glenolia site.

resources.title: Weather, water and decisions: audit a claim
resources.question: How should we judge a confident recommendation built from uncertain environmental data?
resources.summary: Students examine a proposed watering claim, distinguish source types, test calculations and compare monitoring technologies against explicit criteria. The real unscaled moisture report is treated as an information gap rather than a diagnosis. The unit uses simulated data and a simple rainfall-volume model to develop evidence evaluation; it does not prescribe farm irrigation or replace weather/emergency decisions.

resources.title: Living relationships and management choices
resources.question: How can we evaluate a proposed environmental action without claiming an unmeasured benefit?
resources.summary: Students distinguish abundance, richness and distribution in a simplified biological dataset, model possible effects of a proposed management action and compare evidence from different perspectives. They recognise that an environmental value judgement and a scientific claim need different kinds of justification. No local species inventory, biodiversity gain, regenerative practice or farm-management result is established by the unit.

resources.title: Grower to community: trade-offs behind a claim
resources.question: What would we need to compare two supply choices fairly?
resources.summary: Students examine source provenance, compare stakeholder perspectives and audit simplified cost/distance models. They discover that a familiar slogan such as local or efficient does not settle every environmental, economic or social question. The product chain is fictional, and the actual developing coffee trial is never represented as current estate-grown stock, an operating café or a confirmed supplier relationship.

resources.title: Design decisions: criteria, sensitivity and evidence
resources.question: Can a high score hide a weak design decision?
resources.summary: Students develop and evaluate a paper interpretation/display design for a hypothetical learning place. They use explicit constraints, a weighted decision model and a small usability test, then examine how changing priorities can reverse a ranking. The focus is transparent reasoning and an evidence-led revision, not certification of actual access, materials, construction or safety.

resources.title: Evidence portfolio: defend, moderate and revise
resources.question: How can a report communicate learning with the right level of confidence?
resources.summary: Students select individual evidence, audit provenance and uncertainty, compare fictional responses against task criteria and defend a revised explanation. The portfolio becomes a concise account of what was actually demonstrated and what needs another opportunity. It does not convert attendance, login time, uploaded pages or group success into an automatic official grade or competency credential.

resources.title: A place-based investigation with a defensible sampling frame
resources.question: Which permitted observations could represent a clearly defined growing-place question?
resources.summary: Negotiate a biological question about a school-ground environment or a source-based growing context. Students define a sampling frame, evaluate selection and measurement bias and explain the limits of generalisation. The real 27-plant pilot supplies context, not an assumed random or replicated design.

resources.title: Plant response: a careful experimental proposal
resources.question: What design would distinguish a light-related pattern from plausible alternatives?
resources.summary: Students design a teacher-approved biological investigation concerning comparable plants and suitable light conditions. They evaluate allocation, replication, response definition, confounds and welfare, then interpret a labelled simulation or genuinely collected classroom results. Planning does not count as conducting, and farm trial plants are not experimental material.

resources.title: Soil and water models: evaluate validity
resources.question: Which parts of a soil-water question can a simplified apparatus actually answer?
resources.summary: Students compare model methods and operational definitions, examine repeated recovery/flow information and evaluate validity before interpreting biological or agricultural meaning. No unknown soil culture, chemical analysis or real farm treatment is part of this guide.

resources.title: Environmental time series with missing information
resources.question: How can an environmental record inform a biological question without disguising uncertainty?
resources.summary: Students examine timing, instrument metadata, missingness and competing explanations in environmental observations. A single dated owner report is compared with what a genuine repeated record would require. The focus is biological relevance and data quality, not automated crop diagnosis or weather-safety decisions.

resources.title: Habitat relationships and competing explanations
resources.question: What evidence would strengthen a proposed explanation of a biological relationship?
resources.summary: Students build and critique a biological relationship model using reliable sources or low-impact permitted observations. They distinguish abundance, richness and distribution and consider alternative explanations for an apparent environmental change. No local wildlife inventory, species identity or conservation benefit is supplied by character art or a limited photograph.

resources.title: Plant-product provenance: what kind of evidence is needed?
resources.question: Which biological or production claims can be verified from the available sources?
resources.summary: Students examine the evidence behind plant identity, cultivation and product-origin claims. They distinguish a biological question from branding or retail information and evaluate what records, methods or published studies could support a particular assertion. The real trial’s unresolved NR25 identity and unconfirmed harvest remain explicit; no genetic testing or product certification is undertaken.

resources.title: Monitoring design: evaluate a biological information system
resources.question: How would we know whether a monitoring system is fit for a biological question?
resources.summary: Students specify the information needed for a biological investigation and compare manual and automated approaches. The design considers calibration, sampling, maintenance, missing data, access and failure modes. It is a paper/system proposal, not an installed sensor network, automated treatment decision or equipment purchase.

resources.title: An evidence argument for a scientific audience
resources.question: How can a final report be reproducible, critical and proportionate?
resources.summary: Students curate an individual evidence argument, audit source/resource versions and defend a conclusion against an alternative explanation. They respond to teacher moderation and make a specific revision. The outcome is a negotiated project report, not automatic achievement, a new measurement, formal accreditation or a substitute for school assessment requirements.
